systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

ARTICLE :
FINITE-TIME SINGULARITY FORMATION
FOR THE THREE-DIMENSIONAL EULER EQUATIONS
LEVENT ALP ¨OGE, TRISTAN BUCKMASTER, AND MATEI P. COICULESCU
Abstract. We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible
Euler equations whose solution blows up in ﬁnite time. The velocity remains bounded, while the
vorticity magnitude at the origin tends to inﬁnity. Away from the origin, the velocity and its
time derivative have smooth spatial limits at the singular time. The construction uses localized
Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks of a multi-scale construction.

1. Introduction
The incompressible Euler equations are among the earliest partial diﬀerential equations derived
in mathematical physics. Euler presented them in 1755, less than a decade after d’Alembert derived
the wave equation for the vibrating string [41, 42].
The goal of this work is to construct smooth initial data for the incompressible Euler equations
on the three-dimensional torus whose solution blows up in ﬁnite time. We represent T3 by the cube
[−1/2, 1/2]3 with periodic boundary conditions (opposite faces identiﬁed). We write these equations
as
(1.1) ∂tu + (u·∇)u + ∇p = 0, div u = 0 on T3 × [0,T∗).
Local existence and uniqueness for suﬃciently regular data go back to Lichtenstein and G¨unther in
the 1920s [43, 44]. Classical theory on T3 supplies a unique maximal smooth solution from smooth
divergence-free data [13, 10]. By the Beale–Kato–Majda criterion [9, 11], a smooth solution on [0,T )
continues smoothly through T <∞ if

In two dimensions the scalar vorticity is transported, so its L∞ norm is conserved, and smooth
solutions exist for all time [45]. Yudovich [46] proved global existence and uniqueness for bounded,

Numerical searches for blow-up include the Taylor–Green vortex study of Morf, Orszag and
Frisch [48] and Kerr’s computations for antiparallel vortex tubes [49]. In a later computation, Hou
and Li [50] observed at most double-exponential growth of the maximum vorticity past Kerr’s
predicted singular time. Luo and Hou [51] found numerical evidence for axisymmetric blow-up at
the wall of an axially periodic cylinder. Childress, Gilbert and Valiant [52] studied, analytically and
numerically, eroding vortex dipoles in axisymmetric ﬂow without swirl, whose maximal vorticity
grows like t4/3, and Childress and Gilbert [53] proposed, by formal asymptotic analysis, the hairpin
geometry as a model for ﬁnite-time blow-up.
On R3, Elgindi [15] constructed ﬁnite-time blow-up from C1,α0 initial data for some α0 > 0.
Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi [16] obtained stable, locally self-similar blow-up for ﬁnite-energy

axisymmetric data in a periodic cylinder with boundary, using computer-assisted estimates. The
theorem below concerns smooth periodic data on T3, with bounded velocity and vorticity growth
concentrated at the origin.

We construct a sequence of smooth approximate solutions of the Euler equations whose residuals
tend to zero. The sequence converges in every spatial Cm norm, uniformly on compact time intervals
before T∗, to a solution of the Euler equations.
At each step in the sequence we add an oscillation at a higher frequency, localized near the
origin and initially small in velocity. The velocity gradient of the preceding scales ampliﬁes the new
oscillation, whose gradient in turn drives the growth of the next one. The growth intervals have
ﬁnite total length. This multiscale construction follows the approach of C´ordoba and Mart´ınez-Zoroa
for the Euler equations with forcing and for forced IPM [18, 19]. C´ordoba, Mart´ınez-Zoroa and
Zheng [17] used a cascade of vorticity layers to obtain blow-up for the unforced Euler equations on
R3 from C1,α data smooth away from the origin. Related constructions give blow-up with forcing
for the inviscid Boussinesq equations, the variable-density Euler equations and the hypodissipative
Navier–Stokes equations [20, 21, 22]. Our companion papers proving singularity formation for forced
IPM, the forced Boussinesq equations, and the forced Euler equations [3, 1, 2] use forces smooth
in space and time up to the singular time. In the present construction we use Craik–Criminale
waves as building blocks and choose the initial velocity at each step so that the limiting solution is
unforced.
Convex integration constructions of nonunique weak solutions of the Euler equations also use
oscillations at successive frequency scales. Below the Onsager exponent, this method yields solutions
with nonconstant kinetic energy [23, 6]. For the unforced Euler equations in the plane, Coiculescu [24,

nonuniqueness of unforced Leray–Hopf solutions.

The periodic construction starts from the stationary shear ﬂow
U0(x) = sin(2πx2)(e1 + ρe3),
where ei are the coordinate vectors and ρ > 0 is small. It solves the Euler equations with zero
pressure. In the initial coordinate frame its central gradient has ν = 2π and η = 2πρ, so that ε = ρ.
Its explicit ﬂow supplies the ﬁrst wave; subsequent waves use the successive gradients they create.
Craik–Criminale waves on R3 provide a local model for ampliﬁcation. For the periodic construction,
we localize each wave by a smooth cutoﬀ supported in the interior of a fundamental cell in Lagrangian
coordinates. We extend the localized ﬁeld periodically and transport its phase and cutoﬀ by the
preceding periodic velocity, as in geometric optics [37, 38, 39, 40]. Since the cutoﬀ vanishes near
the cell boundary, the wave vector need not lie in Z3. Localization and the spatial variation of the
background introduce errors, which the corrections below make small at each step and remove in
the limit.
1.2. Controlling corrections in an amplifying ﬂow. To correct a velocity in an amplifying
ﬂow, we use the freedom to choose its initial value. To avoid exciting growing modes, we prescribe
the ﬁnal particle positions and choose the initial velocity to reach them.

the particle that starts at a. It satisﬁes
∂tX(t,a) = u(t,X(t,a)), X(0,a) = a.
